newsitem.title: FRANCE: Europe grains prices slip further as harvest looms.
newsitem.headline: Europe grains prices slip further as harvest looms.

text.p: Most European grain prices slipped further this week in dull trade, undermined by slack demand and farm selling ahead of the new harvest, dealers said.

Grain markets largely ignored news the European Union had scrapped controversial export taxes on wheat and flour, replacing them with a "nil value" entry, as brokers said that even without tax EU wheat was not competitive on world markets.
"This goes in the right direction. But this is not enough to export," one French dealer said.
The move had also been expected in the face of lower world prices and prospects for a large crop in the EU.

In France subdued demand pushed old-crop wheat into Rouen to 795 francs per tonne, down 20-25 francs over last week. New crop prices also drifted lower on favourable weather and sluggish export prospects.
Barley trade was very quiet while maize prices edged slightly higher on a lack of sellers.
Farmers are bracing themselves for an early harvest as warm weather had accelerated crop development.

Dry and hot weather over the past 10 days had also revived drought fears in the Beauce grain belt in central France, but showers and lower temperatures forecast for the weekend were expected to provide relief.
May rains helped crops north of the Loire river recover after nearly four months of drought, but the situation in the south looked more grim, the farm ministry said this week.
French brokers played down news the EU had abolished taxes on wheat and flour exports, saying that export rebates were needed to give EU wheat a chance to compete against cheaper world supplies.

In addition the latest U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) estimates of a larger than expected U.S. winter wheat crop were bearish for world prices, further strengthening the case for restoring subsidies on EU wheat exports, they said.
"French wheat is still too expensive to compete with soft red winter wheat now below $140 per tonne," one dealer said.

Exporters and French grain officials have urged the EU to quickly resume exports but the Commission has so far failed to respond, carefully avoiding launching the mechanism for new crop grain export tenders.

In Germany fading demand ahead of the new harvest also pushed down old crop prices this week. Good crop weather, notably above-average rain for May, also put pressure on new crop prices. Trading in barley and rye was very quiet.
Spot bread wheat prices on the Hamburg grain exchange were off five marks per tonne on the week to 272.50 marks and the feed wheat price was also off five at 270.

Old crop barley indications were 260.00 marks, down 2.50 over last week, while new crop barley was unchanged at 240.00. Old crop rye was unchanged at 260.00 and new crop at 252.50, down 2.50 on the week.
Trading in the British grain markets was subdued this week with steady to slightly lower prices as sellers and buyers kept to the sidelines.
No significant business was reported in the fob market while delivered business was conducted in tight ranges.
Italian durum wheat prices were steady while farm selling and scarce buyers drove soft wheat and maize prices down over the past week, the Italian Institute for Agriculture Studies said.

In Spain grain prices, except maize, eased ahead of the new harvest. There were no indications for durum wheat due to a lack of trade but dealers said durum wheat quality had deteriorated due to recent rainfall.
